messages.subject: Gaussian Process Models and map2stan
parts:
Hi all,

 

This is my first time posting here. So thank you for your patience. I am trying to modify code from Richard’s statistical rethinking course to use with my own data (I am hoping some of you are familiar with this code). He provides code to run a Gaussian process model investigating spatial autocorrelation in Oceanic tools. In attempting to modify the code for my own data I have run into two issues.

 

First, in his example there is only one observation per island. With my data I have multiple observations per island (site) and need to modify the model to incorporate that. He explains how to do it in the book, but doesn’t actually provide the code. So, how can I modify the map2stan code to include multiple observations per island?

 

Second, the outcome variables in this example (total tools) are all positive integers. In my data, the outcome variables are the result of PCA, so are positive, negative and are not integers. Do I need to use a different distribution (besides poisson) for my data? Do you have any other thoughts on how to deal with this issue? Thanks so much and here is the code from Richard:

 

 

 

## R code 13.29

# load the distance matrix

library(rethinking)

data(islandsDistMatrix)

 

# display short column names, so fits on screen

Dmat <- islandsDistMatrix

colnames(Dmat) <- c("Ml","Ti","SC","Ya","Fi","Tr","Ch","Mn","To","Ha")

round(Dmat,1)

 

 

## R code 13.31

data(Kline2) # load the ordinary data, now with coordinates

d <- Kline2

d$society <- 1:10 # index observations

 

m13.7 <- map2stan(

    alist(

        total_tools ~ dpois(lambda),

        log(lambda) <- a + g[society] + bp*logpop,

        g[society] ~ GPL2( Dmat , etasq , rhosq , 0.01 ),

        a ~ dnorm(0,10),

        bp ~ dnorm(0,1),

        etasq ~ dcauchy(0,1),

        rhosq ~ dcauchy(0,1)

    ),

    data=list(

        total_tools=d$total_tools,

        logpop=d$logpop,

        society=d$society,

        Dmat=islandsDistMatrix),

    warmup=2000 , iter=1e4 , chains=4 )

 

## R code 13.32

precis(m13.7,depth=2)

Hello,

I have attached a PDF of the relevant chapter from Richard's book. 

In terms of my own data, I have attached a histogram of the distributions of two predictor variables and two outcome variables. Basically, I want to see if gibbon vocalizations (as measured by principle components) from different sites are correlated with some aspect of the ecology at each site (for example, measures of ambient acoustics: acoustic evenness (AEI) and acoustic diversity (ADI)). But, since sites that are closer together are going to be more similar, I have to control for spatial autocorrelation, which is why I want to use a gaussian process model. I have observations of multiple gibbons from each site, and I am not sure how to modify the original code provided to do that.

I hope that is clear. Thanks so much!

Sincerely,
Dena

messages.author: a2bfdf24157fa01a
messages.subject: Re: Gaussian Process Models and map2stan
parts:
Hi Dena,

First: Richard's package is a really convenient way to quickly implement models from R to Stan, but it is quite limited and not too difficult to break.  For more complex models such as yours, it might be well worth the investment to learn to code a Stan model directly. The Stan development team has great packages to use with R (rstan and shinystan), as well as an active forum to get help. Coding the model directly opens up a lot more flexibility and robustness.

Second: While Stan is fast, it can struggle with GP models with lots of observations. For reference, a GP model with reasonable complexity and 1600 observations took several hours to fit running in parallel on 8 cores.  A much faster alternative is Aki's GPstuff. There is an interface so you can use it straight from R.

Assuming you want to continue to use Richard's package:

- Replace the Poisson distribution with one that makes sense for your data (e.g. - normal). Make sure you add code for the additional required parameters (e.g. - sigma).
- I believe the GPL2 function uses a distance matrix as input. You can calculate this in R to hand to map2stan, but make sure to convert to a matrix from the default output for dist(). Stan does not like the vector representation of matrices.
- If you have multiple observations from the same location, the GPL2 should account for this automatically with the jitter included in the L2 function. (Observations with the same distance have a little noise added to avoid perfect correlations.) I believe the last variable in the GPL2 function is the jitter amount (not 100% sure without looking it up).

Hope that helps,

Matt
